title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
hook: Sample the model many times, let each run reason its own way, then take the majority answer - diverse reasoning paths vote out individual errors.
key_points: Generates multiple chain-of-thought responses with temperature > 0, then picks the most common final answer by majority vote.
Consistently outperforms greedy single-path chain-of-thought across arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks.
No additional training, fine-tuning, or external tools required - just repeated sampling.
Cost scales linearly with the number of samples; diminishing returns set in after roughly 20-40 samples.
content_html: Wang and colleagues at Google Brain (2022) proposed self-consistency: instead of trusting one chain-of-thought answer, sample many reasoning paths and take a majority vote on the final answer. The intuition is that wrong paths tend to disagree with each other while correct paths tend to converge.
extra_html:
How it works

You prompt the model with chain-of-thought instructions and a non-zero sampling temperature, collect a set of independent responses (each containing its own reasoning chain and final answer), then aggregate by majority vote over just the final answers - ignoring the intermediate reasoning. No specialized decoding or model changes are needed. The diversity of paths effectively marginalizes over reasoning errors that happen to cluster differently from correct solutions.

Why it matters

Self-consistency is one of the simplest ways to improve reasoning accuracy on tasks where ground-truth answers are unambiguous: you trade inference compute for reliability. It also highlights that model uncertainty at the reasoning level is real and exploitable - a theme that influenced later work on best-of-n sampling and process reward models. The Wang et al. paper on arXiv reports results across a broad sweep of benchmarks and model sizes.

flashcards.prompt: What is the core intuition behind self-consistency?
flashcards.back_html: Wrong reasoning paths tend to disagree with each other while correct ones converge, so sampling many paths and taking a majority vote on the final answer beats trusting one.

flashcards.prompt: When aggregating self-consistency samples, what is the majority vote taken over?

choices.text: Only the final answers, ignoring the intermediate reasoning
The full reasoning chains, matched token by token
The model's logits at each decoding step

flashcards.explanation_html: You collect independent responses with non-zero temperature and vote over just the final answers, not the chains.

flashcards.prompt: What is the main cost tradeoff of self-consistency?
flashcards.back_html: Cost scales linearly with the number of samples, and returns diminish after roughly 20-40 — you trade inference compute for reliability.
